opus-5.5.text:
I think it cuts a couple of ways, and I try not to read too much into it in either direction.

On one hand, it's a bit of evidence that their views aren't purely a reaction to the latest exciting demo. If someone like Shane Legg was saying something like "2028, maybe" back in the late 2000s, before deep learning had really taken off, and then the world has unfolded in a way that looks at least roughly compatible with that, that's somewhat impressive. It suggests they had some model of the situation, whether it's about compute trends or about how hard intelligence really is, that has held up better than a lot of people expected. So you might want to give their reasoning more weight than you'd give someone who only got excited in 2023.

On the other hand, there's a pretty obvious selection effect. The people who ended up founding and leading AI labs are disproportionately people who believed early on that AI was coming soon and would be a huge deal. That's partly why they went into it. So when you look at the people at the top of these organizations, you're looking at a group that was filtered for having short timelines in the first place. That doesn't mean they're wrong, but it means "the leaders of AI labs think AI is coming soon" is less informative than it might sound. It's not like we sampled random thoughtful people and they converged on that view after looking at the evidence.

And relatedly, if your views were already set before most of the relevant evidence came in, then the recent progress isn't really what's driving your beliefs. You might be right, but it's harder to say you're updating on the evidence rather than finding the evidence agreeable. Someone who's always been confident that it's five to fifteen years away is going to look prescient at some point if it happens, and you'd want to know how many other people were confidently predicting things that didn't happen.

So my overall take is: it's mild evidence that they have a decent model, and it's a good reason not to dismiss them as just being caught up in hype. But it's also a reason to be careful about treating their confidence as an independent signal, because they're not a neutral sample, and they've got strong incentives and identities tied up in this view. I'd rather look at their actual arguments and see whether those hold up, and also look at what broader groups of researchers think, which is part of why we do the surveys.

r001.rationale: The response says AI lab leaders are disproportionately people who believed early that AI was coming soon and that this selection makes their views less representative than a broader group. It frames that as a selection effect explaining why their short timelines may differ from broader opinion.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a genuinely interesting piece of evidence, and I'm a bit torn about which way it cuts.

One reading is that these are people who were paying close attention early, saw something real that the rest of us missed, and have since been vindicated. On that story, the fact that they said "this is coming fast" back when it looked crazy, and then it did come fast, should raise our credence in their judgment going forward. Track record matters, and theirs looks pretty good.

But there's another reading that I think deserves more weight than it usually gets. If someone's timeline hasn't moved much across a decade in which an enormous amount has happened, that's a little suspicious in itself. You'd expect a well-calibrated forecaster to update, sometimes up, sometimes down, as evidence comes in. If the number stays roughly fixed regardless of what the world does, that suggests the belief might be coming from somewhere other than the evidence. Maybe a prior about how hard intelligence is, or a sense that it's the kind of thing one ought to think, or just a vision they were drawn to before they had much data. And then the question becomes: were they right because they saw clearly, or were they right somewhat by luck, the way someone who always predicts rain will eventually have a good week?

There's also a selection effect worth noticing. The people who had short timelines were disproportionately the ones who went and founded or joined these labs. So when we look at "leading AI lab figures" and find they held short timelines early, we're partly just observing who chose to work on this. The people with long timelines went and did something else, and we don't put them on podcasts. That doesn't make the short-timeline people wrong, but it does mean the correlation between "is a lab leader" and "had short timelines" is less informative than it first appears.

And then, of course, they're now in a position where short timelines are good for them in various ways. That doesn't mean they're being insincere. I think most of them believe what they say. But I'd be cautious about treating the persistence of the view as strong evidence, when the view has become comfortable to hold.

So on net: I'd give them some credit, because the world did move in the direction they said. But I'd want to see how they've actually updated on specifics, not just whether the headline number survived. Someone who had short timelines for the right reasons should be able to tell you which developments surprised them and which didn't. If nothing surprised them, I'd worry a little.

r001.rationale: The response identifies selection into AI lab leadership and podcast visibility: short-timeline people disproportionately joined or founded labs, while long-timeline people did other things and receive less attention. This explains why lab figures may differ from the broader set of experts.

astra-6.text:
I think it makes their short timelines somewhat less informative about recent developments. If someone thought that human-level AI was five years away ten years ago, and they think it’s five years away now, you probably shouldn’t interpret their current view as a strong update based on something they’ve recently seen inside a lab. It might reflect a fairly persistent outlook they have.

But I wouldn’t take that as evidence that they’re necessarily wrong now. Someone can have been too early and still be right about what’s coming next. I’d want to know what their earlier prediction actually was, how it’s changed, and what evidence they think supports it. The fact that they run an AI lab doesn’t, by itself, tell us how much of their forecast comes from privileged information versus beliefs they’ve held for a long time.

r001.rationale: The response says these figures may have a persistent outlook, making their current forecasts less informative about recent lab evidence. It does not explain their disagreement with broader expert opinion as a selection effect.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that cuts both ways. One interpretation is that they understood something important about where the technology was going, and recent progress is evidence that they were right. But it also makes me less inclined to treat their current timelines as an independent response to the latest evidence. If someone thought AGI was quite close before all of this, then hearing that they still think it’s close doesn’t tell you as much about what the recent developments imply.

I’d want to know what their earlier prediction actually was, what it was based on, and how it’s changed. Did they anticipate the kinds of progress we’ve seen? Or has the date stayed roughly the same distance away as time has passed? Those seem like quite different situations. So I wouldn’t dismiss their views, but I’d put more weight on the reasoning and the track record than on the fact that they’re now leading an AI lab.

r001.rationale: The response says prior short timelines may reflect insight and make current views less independent of recent evidence, but it does not interpret this as a selection effect explaining disagreement with broader expert opinion.
